ideas.name: 1. Korean index-reconstitution flow capture (KOSPI200 and KOSDAQ150 regular reviews, plus MSCI Korea additions), run as an overlay on idle spot cash
ideas.mechanism: Passive KOSPI200 and KOSDAQ150 money (domestic ETFs, the National Pension Service's passive mandates, index futures arbitrage baskets) and MSCI-tracking foreign money have to buy additions and sell deletions in the closing auction on the day before the change takes effect. They care about tracking error, not price. The list is public about two weeks before that day. On the other side, before the effective day, are existing holders and some arbitrage desks that sell into the expected flow. On the day itself, the passive funds are the price-insensitive buyers you sell to. The edge should last because passive AUM in Korea keeps growing (domestic ETF AUM grew many times over from 2014 to 2025), so the forced flow grows faster than the arbitrage capital in this small-cap-tilted, partly retail-driven market. Korean stocks also carry no capital gains tax for a retail holder below the large-shareholder threshold, so the account keeps nearly the whole gross edge after the 0.20% sell tax.
ideas.instruments: Kiwoom spot account, Korean common stocks named as additions to KOSPI200 (KOSPI-listed) and KOSDAQ150 (KOSDAQ-listed), and Korean names added to the MSCI Korea Standard index. Long only: deletions are not shorted, because retail stock borrowing is restricted. Optional: a Kiwoom domestic margin loan up to 1.5x for the about 10-day holding window only. Idle cash between events sits in a KRW money-market or CD-rate ETF (e.g. KODEX CD-rate active, 459580, which only exists after 2023; before that, use the 91-day CD rate as the cash return).
ideas.rule: Event calendar: KOSPI200 and KOSDAQ150 regular reviews are semi-annual and take effect the trading day after the June and December futures/options expiry (second Thursday). The constituent change list is published by KRX about 2 weeks earlier, after the close. MSCI quarterly index reviews are announced after the US close about 2 weeks before the last business day of Feb, May, Aug and Nov. (1) Signal date A = the first KRX trading day whose session starts after the announcement timestamp. Use only the publication time of the press release, never the trading date of the list. (2) Entry: at the open auction on A+1, one full day after the information was available, buy every addition equal-weight. Cap at 10 names; if there are more, take the 10 smallest by float market cap on day A-1, because flow per unit of liquidity is largest there. Skip any name whose 20-day average traded value is under 1bn KRW, and skip names already up more than 15% from A-5 close to A close (the flow is already priced in). (3) Sizing: 100% of the spot cash allocated to this sleeve, split equal-weight. Optional 1.5x via margin loan, but only if the margin rate times days held is under 0.1%. (4) Exit: sell the whole position as a closing-auction (단일가) market order on the last trading day before the effective date, the day the index funds buy. No stops. (5) Between events, hold the cash ETF. (6) Cost model: buy commission 0.015%, sell commission 0.015% plus the 0.20% transaction tax, plus slippage equal to half the quoted spread plus 0.10% per side for names under 10bn KRW daily value. Margin interest at the actual Kiwoom rate. (7) Do not trade deletions or front-run predicted additions. Predicting additions needs historical float market caps that are not freely available, and that would add look-ahead risk.
ideas.data: Constituent change announcements: KRX/KRX Index press releases and free news archives (Yonhap, Hankyung, Maeil). Each event's list and the exact publication time have to be transcribed by hand. KOSPI200 data goes back to the 1990s. KOSDAQ150 was launched in 2015, and its predecessor, KOSDAQ Star, has thin and less useful history. MSCI review press releases (msci.com, archive from about 2008 onward). Prices: Yahoo Finance .KS/.KQ daily OHLC. Bias notes: Yahoo is missing some delisted Korean tickers. Additions are rarely delisted within the next 3 weeks, but the event list comes from announcements, not today's universe, and any missing price series has to be recorded as missing and reported. Never drop it silently. If more than 5% of events lack prices, report results both with those events at a -10% return and without them. Yahoo's Korean open prices before about 2010 are sometimes wrong; cross-check against the close and the previous close and drop the open if it falls outside the day's high-low range.
ideas.testable_to_2014: Partly. The KOSPI200 leg can be tested from about 2005 to 2014, which is about 20 semi-annual events and roughly 100-150 additions, with 2015 onward held out. The MSCI leg can be tested from about 2008. The KOSDAQ150 leg only exists from 2015, so it is holdout-only by construction: pre-register it now with the same rule and judge it on 2015 onward alone.
ideas.expected_net: Arithmetic: assume a gross announcement-to-effective abnormal return per addition of +1.5% to +3% (the range in typical Korean and Asian index-effect studies; US S&P additions decayed to near 0-1% after about 2010, so the Korean figure has to be checked out of sample). Round-trip cost is about 0.25% fixed plus 0.2-0.4% slippage, so the net per window is about +0.8% to +2.5% plus about 10 days of market beta. Windows per year: 2 for KOSPI200, 2 for KOSDAQ150 after 2015, and 1-2 meaningful MSCI windows, about 5 in total. Fully deployed, the excess is about 5 x 1.2% = +6%/yr in the middle case, with a range of 0% to +10%. Standalone event Sharpe is about 0.6-1.0 because the trades cluster in time. As an overlay on the cash sleeve, the drawdown contribution is small (one bad window is about -5% to -8% of the sleeve). After a realistic decay on the holdout I would plan on +2% to +5%/yr added to whatever the core sleeve earns, not a standalone engine.
ideas.capital_fit: 10M KRW: works. Even 10 names is 1M KRW each, and the commission is negligible. 50M and 100M KRW: work. Even a full 100M KRW in a name trading 1bn KRW a day is under 10% of one day's value, but keep the 1bn KRW liquidity floor and spread entries over the first 30 minutes if the position exceeds 5% of average daily value. Capacity is not the binding constraint below a few billion KRW.
ideas.fake_risks: (a) Small N: about 20 KOSPI200 events in-sample, with returns clustered within each window, so the effective N is about 20, not 150. A t-stat near 2 is the realistic best case. (b) Hindsight in the event list: transcribing from news can sneak in post-announcement revisions or the effective-date list; use the first published release only. (c) Timestamp look-ahead: if the release came out intraday, entering at that day's open is look-ahead, hence the A+1 open rule. (d) Regime change: the effect may now be fully captured on the announcement day itself (price jumps at the A open, before the entry), which would leave nothing for the A+1 to effective-date window. Test both windows, but pre-register only the stated one. (e) Pre-2014 Korean returns had a strong small-cap and momentum tilt that the additions share; benchmark against the KOSPI/KOSDAQ return over the same days, not against zero. (f) Optional margin can turn a 1% edge into a forced sale in a crash week such as Dec 2008 or Mar 2020.

ideas.name: 2. Calendar-flow leverage tilt on KOSPI200 (turn of month, pre-holiday, and pre-FOMC days), expressed through KOSPI200 mini futures
ideas.mechanism: Return concentrates on days when cash predictably arrives or risk is predictably removed. Turn of month: salary, pension and fund contributions go in, plus window dressing (Lakonishok-Smidt 1988; McConnell-Xu 2008 found it in about 30 of 35 countries, outside the original sample). Pre-holiday: short sellers and market makers reduce inventory before long Korean holidays (Seollal, Chuseok). Pre-FOMC drift: Lucca-Moench 2015 found it for the US, and it spreads to Asia through overnight futures. On the other side are liquidity providers and hedgers who demand compensation for holding inventory across these days. Honest caveat: turn of month is the most robust of the three. Pre-FOMC has largely faded since publication (2016+).
ideas.instruments: KIS futures account: mini KOSPI200 futures (multiplier 50,000 KRW per point, so one contract is roughly 25-40M KRW notional at 2025-26 index levels), front month, rolled on the Monday of expiry week. Base exposure outside tilt days: the futures position sized to the base leverage L_base. Tilt days raise it to L_tilt. Taxed at 11% on annual net gains above 2.5M KRW, with losses netted within the year. Alternative for the base sleeve inside the ISA: KODEX 200 (069500) for 1x tax-free, or KODEX Leverage (122630, from 2010) taxed as an other-type ETF at 15.4%, or 9.9% inside the ISA.
ideas.rule: (1) Base exposure: L_base = 1.0x notional of account equity if the KOSPI200 close on day t-1 is above its 200-day simple moving average, else 0. The trend filter is evaluated on t-1 close and acted on at t close (one full day of delay). (2) Tilt days, all known in advance from the KRX holiday calendar and the published FOMC schedule: TOM = from the close of the 2nd-to-last trading day of the month to the close of the 3rd trading day of the next month. PRE-HOL = the close 2 trading days before a market closure of 2+ weekdays, held to the close of the last day before the closure. PRE-FOMC = the close of the Korean session 1 day before the US FOMC statement day, held to the close of the Korean session on the statement day itself (Korea trades before the US statement). (3) On a tilt day, exposure = L_base + 1.0x, so 2.0x when the trend is up and 1.0x when the trend is down. Rationale: the calendar flow happens in both trend states, but you take smaller risk when trend is down. (4) Execution: all changes as near-close market orders in the regular session; costs 0.003% futures commission plus 1 tick slippage per side. Contracts are rounded down to whole contracts. If the rounded size is 0 because equity is too small, skip the tilt. (5) Margin: keep at least 40% of the required maintenance margin as excess cash in the futures account; if equity falls below that, cut contracts at the next close. (6) Tax: compute 11% on each calendar year's net futures gains above 2.5M KRW, paid in May of the following year from the account.
ideas.data: KOSPI200 daily close from Yahoo (^KS200) back to about 1990 (check its coverage; fall back to KRX index data posted in free news archives or the Bank of Korea ECOS KOSPI series, which has a free API key). Futures roll costs: model them as the risk-free rate minus the dividend yield, using the Bank of Korea 91-day CD rate (ECOS, free key) and an assumed 1.5-2% dividend yield. Holiday calendar: KRX notices and public calendars. FOMC dates: federalreserve.gov. No survivorship issue, because the only instrument is a single index.
ideas.testable_to_2014: Yes. KOSPI200 futures have traded since 1996 and the index series is longer: in-sample 1996-2014, holdout 2015-2026. Mini futures only exist from July 2015, so before that simulate with the big contract's economics scaled continuously (no rounding). Treat the rounding effect as a holdout-period cost check. Pre-FOMC was published with data through 2011, so its in-sample period is the discovery sample; only its 2015+ holdout counts.
ideas.expected_net: Arithmetic: about 7 tilt days a month (TOM 5, plus pre-holiday and FOMC averaged in), about 85 days a year, about 34% of days. If the tilt days' mean daily excess return is about 0.08% versus about 0.02% for other days (US-style concentration; Korea has to be tested), adding +1.0x on those days earns 85 x 0.08% = +6.8%/yr gross. The added variance is 85 x (1.3%)^2 = 1.4%/yr, so the log-growth penalty is about 0.7% plus cross-terms with the base, about 1-1.5%. Costs are negligible, around 0.1%/yr. Futures tax: 11% of gains, so the net tilt contribution is about +3% to +5%/yr if the effect is fully there, and 0 to +2% if it has halved. Base trend sleeve at 1x KOSPI200: historically about 6-9%/yr with a -30% to -40% max drawdown. Whole system: about 8-13%/yr, Sharpe about 0.45-0.6, max drawdown -40% to -50%. Versus a 3x US ETF with a trend filter: likely lower mean, much lower drawdown. It wins on long-run growth only if the US 3x product's realised volatility drag and tax are worse than assumed.
ideas.capital_fit: 10M KRW: marginal. One mini contract is about 25-40M KRW notional, so 10M KRW of equity forces leverage steps of about 3x per contract. The rule cannot be followed exactly; use KODEX 200 plus KODEX Leverage in the ISA instead, accepting 15.4%/9.9% tax on the leveraged part. 50M KRW: workable, with 1-2 contracts as the base. 100M KRW: fine, with granularity of about 0.3x.
ideas.fake_risks: (a) Calendar effects are the classic data-mining zoo; only TOM has a strong record outside its original sample, so pre-register only the three windows above with these exact boundaries. (b) Korea's turn-of-month pattern may differ from the US one (different pension and salary timing; Korean salaries are often paid on the 10th, 21st or 25th). If the in-sample test shows no TOM effect in Korea, abandon the idea, and do not search for a Korean-specific window. (c) Pre-FOMC returns 2015+ are close to zero in the published follow-ups. (d) Futures roll and dividend modelling errors can be bigger than the edge; check with ETF 069500 total return versus the modelled futures. (e) Margin rounding at small capital makes the live result differ from the backtest.

ideas.name: 3. Korean preferred-versus-common share spread rotation (long-only, between two classes of the same company)
ideas.mechanism: Korean preferred shares (우선주) have the same cash-flow claim plus a small dividend premium, but no vote. They trade at a variable discount, typically 10-50%, that widens when foreign and passive buying goes into the common shares (the common is in the indices; the preferred often is not, or has a small weight) and narrows when dividends rise or governance reforms come in. The spread is driven by index and foreign flows that do not care about price, not by fundamentals. On the other side are index funds and foreign investors who must hold the common share. Because retail cannot short in Korea, the only implementable form is to hold whichever class is cheap relative to its own history, staying long the company. That captures part of the spread reversion while keeping the company's equity beta.
ideas.instruments: Kiwoom spot account. Only liquid pairs where both classes trade at least 2bn KRW a day, fixed at the start of each year from data available then. Example of the type: Samsung Electronics 005930/005935, Hyundai Motor 005380/005385, LG Chem 051910/051915, LG Electronics 066570/066575. Holding is CGT-free; switching costs the 0.20% sell tax each time.
ideas.rule: (1) For each eligible pair, compute the log ratio s_t = ln(P_pref / P_common) on daily closes, adjusted for dividends: use adjusted closes, and for pairs with very different dividend yields add the cumulative dividend difference. (2) z_t = (s_t minus its 500-trading-day rolling mean) divided by its 500-day rolling standard deviation, using data through t-1. (3) Hold the preferred if z_{t-1} < -1.0 (pref unusually cheap), the common if z_{t-1} > +1.0, and keep the current holding otherwise (hysteresis band). (4) Execute at the next day's closing auction. (5) The portfolio is equal-weight across eligible pairs, rebalanced to equal weight only once a year to save the sell tax. (6) Benchmark: the same companies held 100% in common shares. Any edge is the difference from that benchmark. (7) Costs: 0.015% commission per side, 0.20% sell tax, and slippage of half the spread plus 0.05%.
ideas.data: Yahoo Finance .KS daily adjusted closes for common and preferred shares; many large pairs have data from about 2000. Survivorship and selection bias cannot be fully removed: Yahoo is missing preferred lines that were later delisted (many small Korean preferreds were delisted for thin float), and choosing pairs that exist today picks the survivors. Mitigation: limit the universe to pairs whose two classes were both in the top 50 by market cap at each annual selection date, using the KRX market-cap rankings published in that year's news. Report as a known residual bias that the backtest may overstate the result.
ideas.testable_to_2014: Partly. Large-cap pairs go back to about 2000-2005, giving roughly 10-15 years in-sample before 2014, with 2015+ as the holdout. The holdout includes a structural break: the 2024 Korean 'value-up' governance programme and dividend reforms that narrowed preferred discounts. That makes the holdout informative, but it is not stationary.
ideas.expected_net: Arithmetic: the spread half-life is typically 6-18 months. Catching a reversion of about 10 log points about once a year per pair gives about +5%/yr gross relative to holding the common. Rotating about 1.5 times a year costs about 1.5 x 0.25% = 0.4%, so the net is about +2% to +4%/yr relative to the benchmark, with large uncertainty, because there are only 4-6 independent pairs. Absolute return is about that of Korean large caps (5-9%/yr) plus that amount: about 7-12%/yr, Sharpe about 0.4, max drawdown about -50%, the same as Korean large caps. It improves the stock-picking leg, not the growth level; as a growth engine it does not beat 3x leverage.
ideas.capital_fit: Works at 10M, 50M and 100M KRW. Large-cap preferreds trade billions of KRW a day, so capacity is not a problem.
ideas.fake_risks: (a) There are few truly independent pairs, so most of the result may come from one Samsung Electronics regime. (b) Survivorship and selection of the pairs, as above. (c) A preferred discount can widen for years (2008-2015 for some pairs), so 'cheap' can stay cheap. (d) Dividend adjustment errors on Yahoo for Korean preferreds are common and can create fake z-score signals; validate against hand-checked dividend records. (e) The 2024 value-up programme may have permanently changed the mean, which makes a 500-day rolling mean wrong for a while.

top_pick: Method 1, Korean index-reconstitution flow capture, used as an overlay rather than a standalone strategy. The growth engine stays a trend-filtered leveraged index position, held as KOSPI200 mini futures in the KIS account or as a US 3x ETF. The futures route uses little capital as margin, so most spot cash stays free in the Kiwoom account for the 4-6 announced reconstitution windows a year. Each window is entered at the open the day after the announcement and exited in the closing auction the index funds trade. It is the only idea here with a clearly named forced buyer and a public schedule, it reaches the investor tax-free, and it uses capacity no institution wants at this size. Expect it to add +2% to +5%/yr, not to transform returns. Methods 2 and 3 are worth testing only after Method 1 passes, and should be dropped without retuning if their pre-registered in-sample tests fail.
honest_ceiling: 30-60% a year is not a realistic expectation by any method I know of. A plan aiming for it at full Kelly leverage has a high chance of ending far below a plain index fund. The arithmetic: Kelly-optimal log growth is g = r + S^2/2, where S is the Sharpe ratio of the whole portfolio and leverage is set to the optimum. (1) Equity index alone: r about 3%, excess return about 5.5%, volatility about 16%, so S is about 0.34, and g at about 2.1x optimal leverage is 3% + 0.34^2/2 = 3% + 5.8% = 8.8%. Unlevered it is 3% + 5.5% - 1.3% = 7.2%. So leverage adds only about 1.6% unless the Sharpe ratio rises. (2) Add a trend filter: an optimistic but defensible S is about 0.5, giving g = 3% + 12.5% = 15.5% before costs at about 2-3x leverage, which is close to a trend-filtered 3x ETF. Subtract the products' financing spread and fees (about 1-2%) and tax (US-listed: 22% on gains, roughly 15-20% of the excess over a 10-30 year horizon, once the 2.5M KRW allowance and years of deferral are counted), so about 10-12% net. (3) Add uncorrelated event overlays: Method 1 with an incremental standalone Sharpe of about 0.5 and Method 2 with about 0.2 after decay take the combined S to about sqrt(0.5^2 + 0.5^2 + 0.2^2), about 0.74, an optimistic best case. Full-Kelly g = 3% + 0.74^2/2 = 3% + 27% = 30%. That is the only arithmetic path to 30%, and it requires full Kelly with perfectly known parameters. With realistic estimation error (the true S is perhaps 60-70% of the backtest figure), run half Kelly: it captures 75% of the excess at the true S. At a true S of about 0.5, g = 3% + 0.75 x 12.5% = 12.4% before costs and tax, and about 9-12% after. If everything works, up to about S = 0.6 true, g = 3% + 0.75 x 18% = 16.5% before tax and about 13-15% after. My central estimate for this investor is 8-13%/yr net; a good outcome is 15-18%; above about 20% sustained over 10+ years needs either luck or a true Sharpe above about 0.9 after costs. Small retail accounts sometimes reach that briefly in micro-cap events, but I cannot design that with free data and no survivorship bias. A drawdown tolerance of -90% does not raise the ceiling: going beyond Kelly lowers long-run growth, it does not raise it.
assumptions_challenged: (1) 'Leverage is how you get to 30-60%.' Leverage only multiplies Sharpe into growth (g = r + S^2/2 at the optimum); beyond Kelly it reduces terminal wealth. The only real lever is raising the Sharpe ratio after cost and tax, and calendar or flow overlays usually add 0.1-0.3 to S, not 1.0. (2) 'Leveraged-ETF rebalancing and intraday momentum are reachable.' The flow is real (Cheng-Madhavan; end-of-day momentum), but testing it needs intraday data before 2014, which free sources do not provide. Daily open/close proxies cannot capture a last-30-minute effect, so I left it out instead of offering an untestable version. (3) 'Merger arbitrage and tender offers are an easy retail edge.' Possibly, but with free data it cannot be tested honestly: completed-deal targets are delisted and missing from Yahoo, so a backtest sees mostly failed deals or is anchored on survivors. Korean tender-offer (공개매수) activity mostly dates from after 2014. (4) 'US-listed leveraged ETFs are the natural vehicle.' For a Korean resident they carry 22% tax, about 0.5% round-trip commission plus FX spread, and an embedded swap financing spread. KOSPI200 mini futures (11% tax, a near-zero commission, financing at the implied risk-free rate) or tax-free Korean domestic-equity holdings are often more efficient, and futures free up spot cash for event overlays. (5) 'The index-inclusion effect is dead.' That is mostly true for S&P 500 additions, but it does not carry over to a smaller market whose passive share is growing fast. It has to be tested there, not assumed in either direction. (6) 'A 2014 split is a clean holdout.' For pre-FOMC drift and turn-of-month, part of the 'in-sample' period is the original discovery sample. Only post-publication data is a real holdout, and published edges typically lose about a third to a half after publication (McLean-Pontiff), so plan with haircut numbers.

ideas.name: 1 (TOP). Three-asset risk-budgeted portfolio with a trend tilt, levered to about half-Kelly with CME micro futures
ideas.mechanism: Three return streams with long, well-documented histories and low correlation to each other: (a) the equity risk premium, paid to whoever bears crash and recession risk; (b) the bond term premium plus the bond's role as a hedge, paid by issuers and by investors who need to hold duration; (c) gold as a crisis and inflation diversifier. Gold has a weak premium, but its correlation to the other two is near zero or negative. Two structural edges sit on top. First, leverage aversion (Asness-Frazzini-Pedersen 2012; Frazzini-Pedersen, Betting Against Beta). Most investors cannot or will not borrow, so they overweight high-volatility assets and leave low-volatility assets such as bonds with a higher return per unit of risk. Futures let this investor buy that cheaper risk and lever it at roughly the T-bill rate. The other side is leverage-constrained institutions and retail investors who chase return by holding concentrated equity. Second, time-series momentum (Moskowitz-Ooi-Pedersen 2012; Hurst-Ooi-Pedersen, 'A Century of Evidence on Trend-Following'). Hedgers, slow-moving capital and behavioural under- and over-reaction leave trends to exploit. Here trend is used only to tilt how much of each premium the portfolio holds, cutting exposure in long bear markets (bonds 1977-81 and 2022, equities 2008, gold 1981-2000), not as a separate bet. The edges should persist because they are risk premia and constraints, not mispricings that can be arbitraged away. Most of the value comes from diversification raising Sharpe, combined with sizing leverage to the growth-optimal level instead of guessing it.
ideas.instruments: All in the KIS overseas futures account. Equity: CME Micro E-mini S&P 500 (MES, $5 x index, about $33-35k per contract). Bonds: CBOT Micro 10-Year T-Note futures (1/10 of ZN, about $11k notional) if KIS lists them; otherwise CBOT Micro 10-Year Yield futures (10Y, cash-settled to yield, about $10 per basis point; check specs and KIS listing); at 100M KRW or more the full ZN ($100k face) also works. Gold: COMEX 1-Ounce Gold futures (1OZ) if KIS lists them; otherwise Micro Gold (MGC, 10 oz, about $40k). Collateral: hold about 40% of equity as USD cash in the KIS futures account (several times initial margin, enough to absorb a 3-sigma day), and the rest in a Korea-listed KRW money-market or CD-rate ETF (for example a KOFR or CD-rate active ETF) in a domestic account. Top up margin when USD cash falls below 25% of equity. Check whether KIS pays interest on USD futures deposits. If it pays nothing, the idle collateral costs about the T-bill rate (3-4% a year), which is the largest hidden cost in this design.
ideas.rule: Data clock: use daily closes at day t (US settlement). Orders execute at the day t+1 close; in the backtest use the t+1 settlement plus costs. (1) Return series per asset i in {E,B,G}: daily excess returns (futures returns, or index total return minus T-bill). (2) Volatility: sigma_i = EWMA standard deviation of daily excess returns with a 60-day half-life, annualised by sqrt(252), floored at 0.8 x the trailing 5-year realised volatility. (3) Trend score f_i = mean of three indicators: 1 if the trailing 63-, 126- and 252-day excess return is greater than 0, else 0. So f_i is one of {0, 1/3, 2/3, 1}. Multiplier m_i = 0.25 + 0.75 x f_i. The portfolio is never fully out of a premium and never short. (4) Risk budgets b = {E: 0.40, B: 0.35, G: 0.25}, fixed before testing. Raw exposure x_i = b_i x m_i / sigma_i, in notional per unit of equity. (5) Portfolio scaling: estimate the 252-day correlation matrix and shrink it 50% toward the identity. Compute the portfolio volatility of x and scale every x_i by k so that ex-ante portfolio volatility = 20% a year. The target is chosen as about 0.4-0.5 of Kelly for an assumed net Sharpe of 0.45-0.5, because full-Kelly volatility equals the Sharpe ratio. Caps: total gross notional at most 4.0 x equity; equity notional at most 2.0 x; gold notional at most 1.2 x. (6) Contracts: n_i = round(x_i x Equity_KRW / (contract notional_i x USDKRW)). Trade only when |n_target - n_held| >= 1 and the relative gap is more than 20% of target (no-trade buffer). (7) Roll to the next contract 5 business days before first notice or last trade, and charge one round-trip per roll. (8) Kill-switch: none. Drawdowns are accepted by design; the vol target already lowers exposure as volatility rises. (9) Tax: book 11% on each calendar year's net realised derivatives gain above 2.5M KRW, converted to KRW at the trade-date rate, with no loss carry-forward. Costs in the backtest: commission per contract per side at KIS's actual published overseas-futures rate (check it; assume $2.5 per micro contract including exchange fees if unknown), plus 1 tick of slippage per side, plus the FX conversion spread on margin top-ups.
ideas.data: All free. Equities: Ken French daily market excess return (1926-), or S&P 500 from Yahoo ^GSPC (1927-) with dividends from Shiller's monthly file. T-bills: FRED DTB3 (1954-). Bonds: FRED DGS10 (1962-); build daily excess returns as (y_{t-1} - rf_{t-1})/252 - D_mod x (y_t - y_{t-1}) + 0.5 x C x dy^2, with D_mod and convexity of a 10-year par bond at yield y. Gold: LBMA/World Gold Council daily or monthly free series (1968-); Yahoo GC=F (2000-) only as a cross-check. FX: FRED DEXKOUS (1981-) for KRW conversion and tax. Bias notes: no single stocks, so no survivorship bias. The synthetic bond series ignores futures delivery-option and basis effects (small, about 0.1-0.3% a year). Gold before 1975 was not freely traded, so start the joint test in 1975. Micro contracts exist only from 2019 (MES) and later for the micro Treasury and 1-ounce gold contracts, so the backtest uses underlying indices with a full-size-equivalent cost model plus integer-contract rounding at the stated capital.
ideas.testable_to_2014: Yes. Design and calibration window 1975-2014: it covers the 1977-81 bond bear market, the 1980-2000 gold bear market, 1987, 2000-02 and 2008. Holdout 2015-2026 untouched; it includes 2022, the worst stock-plus-bond year in decades. Pre-register every parameter above. Allowed sensitivity runs: vol target {15, 20, 25, 30}% and budgets with gold at {0.15, 0.25}, all reported, none selected after seeing the holdout. Use the micro instruments' real costs only in the holdout years when they existed.
ideas.expected_net: Forward Sharpe assumptions, conservative and below the in-sample history: equity 0.35, 10-year bond 0.20, gold 0.15. With roughly zero average correlation the risk-weighted combination gives S = (0.4x0.35 + 0.35x0.20 + 0.25x0.15)/sqrt(0.4^2 + 0.35^2 + 0.25^2) = 0.2475/0.587 = 0.42. A trend tilt credit of +0.03 to +0.08 gives S of about 0.45-0.50 before costs, and about 0.42-0.47 after costs. At 20% volatility: arithmetic excess return 0.45 x 20% = 9.0%; variance drag 0.2^2/2 = 2.0%; excess log growth about 7%. Add collateral yield of about 2.5-3.5% (USD and KRW cash mix; zero if the broker pays nothing on USD) for about 9.5-10.5% pre-tax log growth. Costs at 100M KRW: about 15-25 contracts, rolls plus rebalances of about 150-250 contract-sides a year at $3-4 each, roughly 0.7-1.0M KRW, or 0.7-1.0% a year. At 50M KRW the cost is about 1.2-1.5%. Tax: 11% of (gain - 2.5M KRW); on a 9% gain on 100M that is 0.715M, or 0.7%. Net expected log growth about 8-9% at 100M KRW and about 7-8% at 50M KRW, with a plausible range of 4-13%. Annual volatility about 20%. Expected worst drawdown over 30 years about -40% to -55%. At a 30% volatility target, excess log growth is 0.45x30 - 4.5 = 9% (versus 7%), so the net gain is about +1.5% for about 1.5x the drawdown. 30% is roughly where the curve flattens if the true Sharpe is 0.45, and it falls if the true Sharpe is 0.35.
ideas.capital_fit: 10M KRW: does not work. One MES contract is about 4.8x equity, so the risk budgets cannot be met and lumpy contracts dominate the risk; use method 2 instead. 50M KRW: works, but coarse. About 1 MES, several micro 10-year contracts and several 1-ounce gold contracts; the equity sleeve is stuck at 0 or 1 contract (0 or about 1x notional), and costs are about 1.3% a year. 100M KRW: works properly; equity in 1-3 MES contracts, with bond and gold sleeves finely granular.
ideas.fake_risks: (1) Bond bull bias: 1982-2020 flatters every risk-parity backtest. Insist on 1975 start and report 1975-1981 separately; if the edge only exists after 1982, discount it. (2) Gold hindsight: gold is included partly because of 2002-2011 and 2023-2026. Pre-registered weights and reporting the 1980-2000 period separately are the only defence. (3) Equity-bond correlation regime: in an inflationary regime (1970s, 2022) stocks and bonds fall together and Sharpe drops sharply; the trend tilt is meant to help, but it reacts with a lag. (4) Synthetic bond returns versus real futures: check against actual ZN continuous data from 2000-2014. (5) Costs: KIS's real per-contract fee and spreads in the micro 10-year contracts (thin liquidity) could be two or more times the assumption. (6) No loss carry-forward plus 11% tax: a loss year followed by a gain year is taxed on the gain in full, which adds about 0.2-0.4% a year of drag beyond the headline rate. (7) USD cash earning 0 at the broker silently removes about 1.5% a year. (8) Any parameter tuned on the holdout invalidates the test.

ideas.name: 2. The same risk-budgeted three-asset portfolio built from US-listed leveraged ETFs (for 10-50M KRW), with low turnover and the 2.5M KRW tax deduction harvested each year
ideas.mechanism: Same premia and the same leverage-aversion logic as method 1. The leverage is bought inside daily-rebalanced leveraged ETFs, so the investor's maximum loss is limited to the capital invested and lumpy contracts are not a problem. The other side is the swap and futures dealers who finance the ETFs (paid about SOFR plus a spread) and, as in method 1, leverage-constrained holders of concentrated equity. Daily-rebalanced leverage is the same as a constant-leverage portfolio, which is what Kelly sizing assumes. The ETF's path dependence is a property of constant leverage, not a hidden cost.
ideas.instruments: Kiwoom overseas spot account. UPRO (3x S&P 500); TMF (3x ICE US Treasury 20+ Year; its duration is about 17 x 3, so size it in volatility units, not notional), or TYD (3x 7-10 year Treasury, closer to a 10-year exposure but thin; check liquidity and that it is still listed); UGL (2x gold); remaining cash in SGOV or BIL (0-3 month T-bills). Not suitable for the ISA, which cannot hold US-listed products. Korean-listed leveraged products cannot replicate this cheaply: 2x at most, synthetic, and taxed at 15.4%.
ideas.rule: Compute the target per-asset notional exposures X_E, X_B, X_G exactly as in method 1 steps (2)-(5), with three changes. Evaluate monthly on the last trading day using day t closes, and trade at the t+1 close. Vol target 20%. Bond volatility is measured on the 20-year-plus index if using TMF. ETF weights: w_UPRO = X_E/3, w_TMF = X_B/3, w_UGL = X_G/2. If w_UPRO + w_TMF + w_UGL > 1, scale all three down proportionally to sum to 1 (the leverage cap); otherwise put the remainder in SGOV. Trade a sleeve only when its weight differs from target by more than 25% relative or 5 percentage points absolute, whichever is larger. This deliberately cuts realisations to about 2-6 trades a year. Tax harvest: in each December, if the year's realised net overseas-equity gain is below 2.5M KRW, sell and immediately rebuy enough appreciated lots to realise gains up to 2.5M KRW, and harvest losses against gains likewise. (Korea is understood to have no wash-sale rule for overseas stocks; verify.) Tax in the backtest: 22% of (net realised gains for the year, KRW, minus 2.5M), with no carry-forward; unrealised gains taxed only at the final liquidation in the last year (report both before and after final liquidation). Costs: 0.25% commission per side (0.07% as a sensitivity case), plus half the quoted spread, plus about 0.1% FX conversion each way on net KRW flows.
ideas.data: Synthetic leveraged-ETF returns from free indices: r_LETF,t = L x r_index,t - (L-1) x (rf_t + s)/252 - ER/252, with s = 0.5% (equity swap spread) and ER = 0.9-1.0%. S&P total return as in method 1 (1927-). 20-year Treasury from FRED DGS20 (1962-1986, then 1993-; fill 1987-1992 with DGS30, or use DGS10 with duration scaling). Gold as in method 1 (1975-). Validate the synthetic model on 2009-2014 actual UPRO/TMF/UGL prices from Yahoo, inside the calibration window. Required: tracking error under 1.5% a year and mean drift within plus or minus 0.5% a year; otherwise change s once and freeze it.
ideas.testable_to_2014: Partly. The instruments themselves exist only from 2008-2009, so 1975-2008 is synthetic; the synthesis is mechanical and checked on 2009-2014. Holdout 2015-2026 is real ETF data. Note that the holdout includes TMF's roughly -75% peak-to-trough fall in 2020-2023, a true out-of-sample stress for the bond sleeve.
ideas.expected_net: Same gross portfolio Sharpe as method 1 (about 0.45), minus extra friction. ETF expense plus swap spread on the levered part is about 0.6-0.8% a year at portfolio level (exposure-weighted), versus about 0.2-0.4% for futures. Commission and FX at low turnover about 0.2-0.3%. Excess log growth about 7.0 - 0.7 - 0.25 = 6.0%, plus T-bill yield on the residual and the yield implicit in the ETFs: total about 9% pre-tax. Tax at 22% with partial deferral and yearly harvesting of the 2.5M deduction gives an effective drag of about 1.0-1.8% a year (deferral helps; rebalancing realisations hurt). Net expected log growth about 7-8%, range 3-12%. Volatility about 20%, worst drawdown about -45% to -60% (ETF path dependence in fast crashes; 2020 and 2022 are the tests).
ideas.capital_fit: 10M KRW: works; it is the only method here that does. 50M KRW: works; compare costs with method 1 and prefer method 1 if KIS micro-futures fees are low. 100M KRW: works, but the 22% versus 11% tax rate and higher internal costs make method 1 better by roughly 1% a year.
ideas.fake_risks: (1) Synthetic returns understate the real ETF swap spread in stressed periods (2008, 2020) and ETF intraday breakdowns. (2) TMF is the 20-year-plus segment, not the 10-year, so duration risk is larger and the 1977-81 bear market is brutal in synthetic tests; that should be reported, not hidden. (3) Tax deferral benefits assume the investor never needs to sell before year 30; the realistic case is somewhere between. (4) The thin liquidity and closure risk of TYD and UGL. Product closure mid-plan forces a taxable switch. (5) Same bond-bull and gold-hindsight biases as method 1.

ideas.name: 3. Diversified multi-market trend-following sleeve in micro futures, added to method 1 at 100M KRW or more (not standalone)
ideas.mechanism: Time-series momentum across many asset classes has the most cross-sample evidence of any trading anomaly (over 100 years and dozens of markets: Hurst-Ooi-Pedersen; Moskowitz-Ooi-Pedersen; Baltas-Kosowski). Its value for a log-growth investor is that it is close to uncorrelated with the long premia in method 1, with positive returns in prolonged crises (2008, 2022). On the other side are commercial hedgers paying for insurance, central banks and institutions that rebalance against trends, and investors who are slow to react to news. It persists because it is a risk-transfer and behavioural effect with crash-like losses at turning points that many investors will not bear. Net Sharpe of professional CTA indices has been about 0.3-0.5 over long periods. A retail version with about 10 markets should be assumed weaker, about 0.3.
ideas.instruments: KIS overseas plus domestic futures accounts. Use micro contracts whose volatility per contract is small relative to 100M KRW: MES, M2K (Micro Russell 2000), Micro Nasdaq (MNQ), KOSPI200 mini futures (KRX, 50,000 KRW multiplier; domestic derivatives are taxed in the same 11% basket; retail pre-education and deposit requirements apply), micro 10-year T-note or micro 10-year yield, Micro 2-Year Yield, 1OZ or MGC gold, MCL (Micro WTI, 100 bbl), Micro FX (M6E EUR/USD 12,500 EUR; M6A AUD/USD 10,000 AUD). Exclude micro silver and copper unless their volatility per contract is under 3% of capital.
ideas.rule: For each instrument j, using day t closes, execute at the t+1 close. sigma_j = 36-day EWMA volatility of daily price changes in money terms per contract, using the back-adjusted continuous series. Raw forecasts: EWMAC(16,64), EWMAC(32,128), EWMAC(64,256), each = (EMA_fast - EMA_slow) / sigma_price_daily. Scale each so its long-run mean absolute value = 10 (scalars fixed from the 1975-2014 pooled sample), cap at plus or minus 20, combine with equal weights, multiply by 1.2 (diversification multiplier for the three correlated forecasts), and cap again at plus or minus 20. Position_j = forecast_j/10 x (sleeve vol target x Equity / N_instruments) / (annualised volatility of one contract in money) x IDM, where IDM = 1.5 (instrument diversification multiplier, fixed). Sleeve vol target = 12% of total equity, with method 1 then run at 16% instead of 20%, so the combined portfolio volatility is about 20% given correlation near 0. Round to integers with a 10% buffer of the unrounded position. Long and short allowed. Roll 5 days before expiry. Costs and tax as in method 1.
ideas.data: Underlying series rather than futures, before about 2000. Equities from Yahoo (^GSPC 1927-, ^RUT 1987-, ^NDX 1985-, ^KS200 1990s-, check the start date). Bonds from FRED yields (constructed as in method 1). Gold LBMA. FX spot from FRED (1971-) plus the interest-rate differential from FRED short rates as carry. WTI spot from FRED DCOILWTICO (1986-). Yahoo =F continuous futures from about 2000 for cross-checks, but they are unadjusted, so splice with back-adjustment. Bias notes: spot crude ignores roll yield (contango), which materially distorts trend results in commodities; treat crude results as indicative only. No survivorship issue: the instruments were chosen for their current micro-contract availability, not past performance.
ideas.testable_to_2014: Partly. Equity indices, bonds, FX and gold from the 1970s-1980s; crude from 1986 and only as spot. Holdout 2015-2026 should use real futures where free data allow. Micro contracts start 2019 or later, so integer rounding at 100M KRW can be simulated only by applying today's contract sizes to historical prices (state this).
ideas.expected_net: Standalone: net Sharpe about 0.25-0.35 at 12% volatility gives about 3-4% excess arithmetic return, about 3% after drag, and about 2-2.5% after costs (higher turnover, roughly 300-500 contract-sides a year at 100M KRW, about 1.0-1.5M KRW). As a sleeve with correlation about 0 to method 1 (S about 0.45), the combined Sharpe = sqrt(0.45^2 + 0.3^2) = 0.54 before extra costs, about 0.50 after costs. At 20% combined volatility that is about +0.8-1.0% a year of log growth over method 1 alone, after costs and 11% tax. Net combined expected log growth about 9-10% at 100M KRW.
ideas.capital_fit: 10M KRW: no. 50M KRW: no; too lumpy, with costs above 2% of capital. 100M KRW: marginal but workable with about 8-10 instruments, each holding 0-3 contracts. Real benefit needs about 300M KRW or more.
ideas.fake_risks: (1) Trend-following's 2011-2019 performance was weak, which signals possible crowding or decay; the holdout is a fair test. (2) Forecast scalars and EWMAC speeds are the canonical published ones, but any re-tuning after seeing results is overfitting. (3) Spot proxies for crude and other commodities overstate trend returns. (4) With 1-3 contracts per market, rounding noise can dominate: simulate it explicitly, not with fractional positions. (5) Short positions in equity index futures carry the equity premium against you; the 2010s showed this cost.

top_pick: Method 1: the three-asset risk-budgeted portfolio (S&P 500, 10-year Treasury, gold) with a 0.25-1.0 trend multiplier per asset, scaled to a 20% volatility target (about 0.4-0.5 of Kelly), held in CME micro futures in the KIS overseas-futures account. It is my top pick because: (a) diversification is the only reliable way to raise Sharpe, and growth rises with Sharpe squared; (b) futures give the cheapest leverage available to this investor (about the T-bill rate, versus 8-9% for Korean margin loans or a 1-2% spread inside leveraged ETFs); (c) gains are taxed at the 11% derivatives rate instead of 22% for overseas ETFs; (d) the whole thing is testable from 1975 with free index and FRED data, with 2015-2026 as a real holdout. It needs about 50M KRW and is good at about 100M KRW. At 10M KRW, use method 2 (the same portfolio in UPRO/TMF/UGL) and switch when capital allows. Before going live, check KIS's actual micro-futures commission, whether it lists micro 10-year and 1-ounce gold contracts, and whether USD futures collateral earns interest. If USD collateral earns nothing, keep most collateral in a KRW money-market ETF.
honest_ceiling: No documented method gets this investor to 30-60% a year as an expected outcome. Here is the arithmetic. For a leveraged portfolio with excess Sharpe S, expected log growth is g = r_f + S x sigma - sigma^2/2. This is maximised at sigma* = S (full Kelly), giving g* = r_f + S^2/2. Because S is only an estimate, a prudent investor runs about half Kelly, which gives r_f + 0.375 x S^2. The after-tax result is roughly 0.89 x g for 11% derivatives tax, or about 0.78-0.85 x g for 22% ETF tax with partial deferral. Costs come off on top. Required Sharpe for a 30% net target: pre-tax g of about 33.7%, minus r_f of 3.5% leaves 30.2% from the Sharpe term. At full Kelly with perfectly known parameters that needs S = sqrt(2 x 0.302) = 0.78. At half Kelly it needs S = sqrt(0.302/0.375) = 0.90, net of all costs and sustained for decades. A 60% target needs S of about 1.1 at full Kelly or about 1.3 at half Kelly. Long-run realities: the US equity market's excess Sharpe is about 0.35-0.40, with 0.30-0.35 a more realistic forward figure. A diversified stock, bond and gold mix with a trend tilt is about 0.45-0.55 in history and about 0.4-0.5 forward. Professional managed-futures indices are about 0.3-0.5 net. Even the best large multi-strategy funds that a retail investor cannot access are about 1.0-2.0, and that comes from capacity-limited, high-turnover strategies with institutional infrastructure. Realistic case for this investor: S of about 0.45 after costs at 20-30% volatility gives pre-tax log growth of 3% + 0.45 x 20% - 2% = 10% (at 20% volatility) or 3% + 13.5% - 4.5% = 12% (at 30% volatility). After 11% tax and about 1% of costs, that is about 8-10% net a year, with a plausible range of about 5-13%. The same formula explains why a plain 3x S&P 500 position is worse than it looks. With S of 0.35 and 17% volatility, the Kelly leverage is about 0.06/0.0289, roughly 2.1x, so 3x is above Kelly: 3.5% + 3 x 6% - 2.1% of costs - 9 x 0.0289/2 = 6.4% pre-tax log growth before any trend filter. A trend filter may lift this to about 9-11% pre-tax, but at the 22% tax rate on frequent realisations that gives about 7-9% net. So the realistic edge of method 1 over that baseline is about 0-2% a year plus much shallower drawdowns, not a multiple of it. Range of outcomes: at 20% volatility, the annualised growth over 20 years has a standard deviation of about 20%/sqrt(20) = 4.5%. The 90th-percentile outcome is therefore about 14-15% a year; a 30% a year outcome over 20 years would be a 4-to-5-sigma event under the model. Over 10 years (standard deviation about 6.3%), the 90th percentile is about 17%. Accepting a -90% drawdown does not change this: going beyond Kelly lowers expected log growth, so willingness to take risk is not the binding constraint; the low Sharpe of the available return streams is. Honest ceiling: about 10-12% a year net of all costs and tax in expectation for a well-built retail portfolio, about 13-15% only if the assumed Sharpe turns out optimistic-but-true at about 0.6, and 30%+ only through luck, not design.
assumptions_challenged: (1) 'More leverage means more growth.' Beyond the Kelly point (volatility equal to the Sharpe ratio), expected log growth falls. On equities alone, 3x is already above Kelly for any realistic forward Sharpe. The investor's -90% drawdown tolerance is not the binding constraint; low Sharpe is. (2) 'Search for a better signal.' Diversifying across a few uncorrelated premia raises Sharpe more reliably than any single-asset timing signal, and growth rises with Sharpe squared. Moving S from 0.35 to 0.5 doubles the achievable excess growth. (3) Risk-parity backtests starting in 1982 are inflated by a 40-year bond bull market; testing must start before 1982 (1975 or earlier) and report 1975-81 and 2022 separately. (4) 'Futures margin cash is free.' If USD collateral at the broker earns nothing, the investor silently loses the T-bill rate on most of the capital; collateral management is worth 1-3% a year. (5) Tax location is treated as an afterthought, but it is first order. The 11% derivatives rate versus 22% for overseas ETFs is worth about 1% a year at 10% growth. Korea's lack of loss carry-forward penalises volatile year-to-year P&L. Deferral (not realising gains) can beat a lower tax rate over 20-30 years, so turnover should be designed around tax. (6) The benchmark '3x ETF with a trend filter' is usually backtested with same-day signals, no tax and understated financing costs. Under one-day delay, the 22% tax on each trend exit and realistic swap spreads, it is much weaker than its reputation. Comparisons must be like for like. (7) Free single-stock data cannot support any cross-sectional stock strategy without survivorship bias. Index-and-futures construction avoids the problem entirely, which is a reason to prefer it, not just a limitation. (8) Small capital (10M KRW) is a hard constraint on futures because contracts are lumpy; it is not a detail to round away.

ideas.name: 1. Tax-bucket and vehicle-routed, Kelly-sized trend exposure (same signal family as the baseline, built from different parts)
ideas.mechanism: This method does not try to win by forecasting better. The baseline (a 3x daily-reset US ETF in the 22% overseas-stock bucket, switched by a trend filter) carries about four avoidable drags. (a) Tax. Every trend exit realises gains at 22%, and there is no loss carry-forward, so a volatile strategy is taxed on its good years and gets no credit for its bad ones. In practice that pushes the effective rate above 22%. Korean law gives SEPARATE 2.5M KRW basic deductions to the overseas-stock basket and the derivatives basket (Income Tax Act art. 103). Derivative gains are taxed at 11%, and KOSPI200 and overseas futures/options are netted against each other inside that basket. The ISA defers tax until maturity, nets gains against losses, exempts the first 2M KRW and taxes the rest at 9.9%. (b) Trading cost. 0.25% per side plus FX spread on 4-8 switches a year is roughly 2-4% a year. A CME micro future costs about USD 2-3 per side on about USD 35k of notional, roughly 0.01%. (c) Leverage comes in 1/2/3x steps instead of a continuous level. (d) Leverage is set without regard to current volatility. Nobody is on the other side of (a) and (b): the gain comes from statute and cost structure, and it lasts as long as the tax law does. For (d), the counterparties are investors who keep fixed leverage through high-volatility regimes. Volatility clusters and the risk-return trade-off is worse when volatility is high (Moreira-Muir 2017), and for the market index this has held up better out of sample than it has for factors.
ideas.instruments: Signal: S&P 500 index. Exposure, filled in this order. (1) KIS overseas futures: CME Micro E-mini S&P 500 (MES, USD 5 x index, about USD 34-35k, roughly 48-50M KRW per contract), derivatives bucket at 11%. (2) Kiwoom ISA: a Korea-listed S&P 500 ETF (e.g. TIGER US S&P500, 360750) for the unlevered part, and a Korea-listed 2x US-index ETF only if one is ISA-eligible (verify; leveraged ETFs require the 1-hour education course and the basic deposit). Taxed at maturity: 2M KRW free, then 9.9%. (3) Kiwoom overseas account: VOO/SPLG (1x) or SSO/UPRO for any residual notional, overseas-stock bucket at 22% with its own 2.5M KRW deduction. Cash and margin collateral are held in USD (USD deposit or SGOV), so the whole position stays USD-unhedged like the baseline. Pre-register a KRW-hedged variant as a secondary test.
ideas.rule: Run daily after the US close. Orders go out at the next session's open, or at the next close for the MOC variant, so there is at least one day of delay. 1) Trend state T_t = 1 if the S&P 500 close > its 200-day SMA AND the close > the close 252 days ago; T_t = 0 if both conditions fail; otherwise keep the previous state (hysteresis). 2) Volatility estimate: sigma_t = annualised EWMA std of daily log returns, halflife 20 days, floored at 8%. 3) Target leverage L_t = T_t * min(3.0, 0.5 * m / sigma_t^2), with fixed m = 0.08 (assumed excess return while the trend is up; set a priori, never fitted). This is half-Kelly: 2.8x at 12% volatility, 1.0x at 20%. 4) Only trade when |L_t - L_held| > 0.3 or T changes. 5) Routing: target notional N = L_t * equity_KRW. a) n_MES = floor((N - ISA_capacity_notional) / MES_notional_KRW), floor 0. b) ISA holds up to the lesser of the ISA balance and N, in 1x or 2x Korea-listed ETFs. c) Any remainder below one MES contract goes into US ETFs at Kiwoom; use the lowest-leverage ETF the available cash allows. 6) MES margin: keep at least 3x the initial margin in USD at KIS. If equity at KIS falls below 2x the initial margin, cut contracts that same day. 7) When T = 0: close futures and leveraged ETFs and hold USD T-bills (SGOV) or USD deposit. ISA money moves to a KRW money-market ETF. 8) Year-end harvesting: in the first half of December, realise gains in the overseas-stock bucket up to 2.5M KRW by selling and immediately buying back (verify that no wash-sale rule applies). If the derivatives bucket's realised gain is below 2.5M KRW and the futures carry unrealised gains, roll or close and reopen to use the rest of the deduction. 9) Roll MES 5 trading days before expiry. 10) Tax engine in the backtest: convert each bucket's realised PnL to KRW at the trade-date FX rate. Then apply 11% to (derivatives net gain - 2.5M), 22% to (overseas-stock net gain - 2.5M), and ISA at maturity (2M free, then 9.9%), with no loss carry-forward, paid from capital each May.
ideas.data: ^GSPC from Yahoo (daily from 1950) for the signal. ^SP500TR (1988-) or Shiller dividends for total return. FRED DTB3 and SOFR for financing. USD/KRW from FRED DEXKOUS (1981-) for KRW conversion and tax. Futures implied financing spread over the T-bill rate: no free history, so assume a constant +0.40%/yr and stress-test at +1.0%/yr. MES exists only from 2019. Before that, simulate contracts of MES size (USD 5 x historical index level) as a hypothetical vehicle. ETF fees and swap spreads come from fund documents: UPRO 0.91% expense, and assume a swap spread of SOFR+0.5% on the borrowed 2x. Index data has no survivorship bias.
ideas.testable_to_2014: Yes for the signal, sizing and the tax and cost engine (1981-2014 in KRW terms, 1950-2014 in USD terms), with 2015-2026 held out blind. Partly for the vehicles: MES (2019) and leveraged ETFs (2009) are modelled synthetically before they existed, and the ISA dates from 2016 (and was redesigned in 2021), so the ISA leg is modelled as a rule. State this plainly in the report. The comparison that matters is baseline vs method on the same synthetic index path, so the vehicle modelling cancels out to first order.
ideas.expected_net: Illustrative, assuming the signal's Sharpe while invested is about 0.45-0.55 with no forecasting improvement. Gross log growth of a half-to-near-Kelly trend exposure: r + about 0.75 * S^2/2 * (Kelly-scaling factor), so about 3% + 7-10% = 10-13%/yr before costs and tax. Drag in the baseline: trading about 1.5-3% (6 switches x 2 x 0.25% + spread + FX), ETF expense and swap about 1.9%, tax about 22-25% of gains on top of that, so the baseline nets about 6-9%. Drag in this method at 100M KRW: trading about 0.1%, futures financing spread about 0.4% x L, tax 11% on derivative gains with two deductions (5M KRW tax-free each year), so it nets about 9-11%. Expected advantage: about +1.5 to +3.5%/yr at 50-100M KRW, and about +0.5 to +1.5%/yr at 10M KRW, where the deductions already make both versions nearly tax-free and most of the gain comes from ISA deferral and lower trading cost. Sharpe after costs about 0.4-0.5. Maximum drawdown: the -55% to -75% range is expected over 30 years (volatility scaling and the trend filter cut 1987/2008-type losses, but a gap like 1987 hits at whatever leverage is held).
ideas.capital_fit: 10M KRW: only partly. One MES is about 5x the account, so no futures. Use ISA plus Korea-listed ETFs plus US ETFs, and the method collapses to baseline + continuous sizing + deferral + harvesting. 50M KRW: works, with 1-3 MES contracts plus ETF residual; lumpiness is about ±0.5x of leverage. 100M KRW: works well, granularity about ±0.25x.
ideas.fake_risks: 1) Any apparent edge from the vol scaling or the 252-day plus 200-day hysteresis has to be checked against the plain 200-day SMA baseline on the SAME vehicles; otherwise the routing benefit and the signal benefit get mixed up. 2) The futures financing spread has been as high as about +1%/yr (2021-2024). If it were 1.5% on 3x notional, the futures route would cost more than ETFs before tax. 3) Tax law can change, and the derivatives tax rate and basket structure are policy choices. Verify current rules with KIS or the NTS, especially whether US-listed ETF options and leveraged Korea-listed ETFs are treated as stated. 4) The ISA 2x product may not exist or may not be eligible. 5) Paying tax from capital each May is a real cash-flow event that a CAGR-only backtest leaves out. 6) A margin call at KIS during an overnight gap is an operational risk that a daily backtest understates.

ideas.name: 2. Judge at the portfolio level: equity-trend core plus a small cross-asset futures trend sleeve, sized jointly for log growth
ideas.mechanism: This drops a judging assumption the team probably made: that each candidate must beat '3x index + trend filter' ON ITS OWN. Under log-growth maximisation, a return stream with low standalone growth but near-zero (or crisis-negative) correlation to the equity core raises the achievable growth r + S_p^2/2. Two uncorrelated streams with Sharpe 0.45 and 0.35 combine to about sqrt(0.45^2 + 0.35^2) = 0.57. Time-series momentum in bonds, FX and commodities is the best documented such stream (Moskowitz, Ooi and Pedersen 2012; Hurst, Ooi and Pedersen's century-of-evidence study). The counterparties are hedgers who pay to shed risk (producers, central-bank-driven FX flows, liability-driven duration buyers) and investors who under-react and then herd. The risk premium for crash convexity should persist because most capital cannot stomach long flat stretches; trend did roughly nothing from 2011 to 2019.
ideas.instruments: All in the KIS derivatives bucket (11% tax, netted together). Equity core: as Method 1 (MES), optionally plus KOSPI200 Mini futures (KRW 50,000 x index). Trend sleeve, small contracts only: CME Micro 10-Year Yield futures (10Y, USD 10 per bp); CME Micro Gold (MGC, 10 oz) or 1-Ounce Gold (1OZ) if KIS lists it; CME Micro WTI (MCL, 100 bbl); KRX USD/KRW futures (USD 10,000) and JPY/KRW futures (JPY 1,000,000); CME Micro EUR/USD (M6E, EUR 12,500). Check each contract's availability and per-contract commission at KIS before freezing the list.
ideas.rule: Run daily after the close, executing the next session. For each sleeve market i (US 10-year rate, gold, crude, USD/KRW, JPY/KRW, EUR/USD): signal s_i = 0.5*sign(r_i,252) + 0.5*sign(r_i,63), using excess returns of the back-adjusted futures or of the proxy series below. Risk: sigma_i = EWMA 60-day annualised volatility. Raw notional_i = s_i * (0.10 / sqrt(6)) / sigma_i * Equity (sleeve vol about 10% before diversification). Contracts = round(notional_i / contract notional_i). Drop market i if a single contract's risk exceeds 2x its target. Only trade when the rounded contract count changes and |target - held| >= 1 contract, held for at least 2 consecutive days to stop flip-flopping. Combination: the equity core uses Method 1 with m and the leverage cap unchanged, and the sleeve is added on top (not taken out of the core) with its risk scale k_s = 1.0, fixed a priori. Total margin across all futures must stay under 35% of equity; if the cap binds, scale the sleeve down first. Roll every contract 5 trading days before first notice or expiry. Tax: one derivatives bucket, 11% above 2.5M KRW, paid each May.
ideas.data: Pre-2014 proxies, all free. US 10-year: build daily total return from FRED DGS10 (1962-) with a duration approximation. FX: FRED DEXJPUS (1971-), DEXKOUS (1981-), DEXUSEU (1999-; use DEXGEUS before that), plus the rate differential from FRED for carry. Gold: World Bank Pink Sheet monthly (1960-) and Yahoo GC=F daily (2000-). Crude: FRED DCOILWTICO spot (1986-) has NO roll yield, so deduct a pre-set 3%/yr contango cost or leave crude out of the pre-2014 test. Cross-check against the AQR 'Time Series Momentum' and 'Century of Evidence' factor files (free, monthly, gross, diversified across 58 markets; treat them as an UPPER bound). No survivorship issue, because the markets are fixed a priori.
ideas.testable_to_2014: Yes in proxy form from 1981 (KRW-based) or 1971 (USD), with 2015-2026 blind. The actual micro contracts mostly launched in 2019-2025 (micro yield 2021, MCL 2021), so contract granularity before then is simulated. Yahoo continuous futures (=F) are unadjusted front-month series, so do not use them for signals without back-adjustment.
ideas.expected_net: Sleeve with 5-6 markets: Sharpe after costs maybe 0.25-0.45 (published trend Sharpe of about 0.7-1.0 on 50+ markets 1985-2012 falls with fewer markets and with post-2011 decay). Correlation with the equity core about -0.1 to +0.1. Combined Sharpe 0.50-0.60 against about 0.45 for the core alone. At half to near Kelly, gross growth rises by about (0.55^2 - 0.45^2)/2 * 0.75 = about 3.8 points in the optimistic case and about 1 point in the pessimistic case. After 11% tax and about 0.3%/yr of sleeve trading cost: an expected +0.5 to +3%/yr over Method 1, with lower maximum drawdown (sleeve gains in 2008 and 2022) but long periods of under-performance (2011-2019).
ideas.capital_fit: 10M KRW: no. Even micro contracts create about 1-3x of single-asset leverage per contract, and the margin cap binds. 50M KRW: marginal; perhaps 3-4 sleeve markets with ±1-contract granularity. 100M KRW: workable, but still coarse; integer rounding is a real source of tracking error and must be simulated exactly.
ideas.fake_risks: 1) Proxy series (spot crude, synthetic bonds) overstate returns. 2) Trend Sharpe has decayed since about 2012, and pre-2014 evidence is mostly from the high-Sharpe era. 3) With only 6 markets, results depend on 1-2 big episodes (2008, 2014 oil, 2022 rates). Bootstrap by year and report the median as well as the mean. 4) Choosing the 252/63 lookbacks or the market list after seeing pre-2014 results reintroduces snooping, so freeze them now. 5) Lumpiness can turn intended risk parity into a portfolio that is mostly one market.

ideas.name: 3. Convex leverage: deep in-the-money long-dated index calls (buy-to-open) in place of a daily-reset 3x ETF while the trend is up
ideas.mechanism: This drops the assumption that leverage must come either from daily-reset ETFs (path decay, no floor) or from margin and futures (margin calls). A deep in-the-money LEAPS call is a stock position financed at roughly the risk-free rate inside the option, plus a far out-of-the-money put that caps losses. The holder pays the variance and skew premium only on the embedded put, which is small when the strike is about 75-80% of spot. Under Korean rules, exchange-traded overseas options appear to fall in the derivatives bucket (11%, netted with futures). That needs confirming for US-listed ETF options specifically. Kiwoom's buy-to-open restriction does not bind, because the method only buys. The counterparties are option market makers and covered-call and overwriting funds that sell long-dated upside. The edge is mainly tax, plus no margin calls and no daily-reset decay, NOT mispricing; the put premium paid is a cost.
ideas.instruments: Kiwoom US options, buy-to-open: SPY or QQQ calls, 9-18 months to expiry, strike about 0.75-0.80 x spot (delta about 0.85-0.90). Cash in SGOV. Derivatives bucket (verify with Kiwoom and the NTS that US ETF options are treated as overseas exchange-traded derivatives).
ideas.rule: Run daily after the close, executing next day with limit orders at mid + 25% of the spread. Use Method 1's trend state T_t and target leverage L_t. When T = 1: hold calls with total delta-notional = L_t * Equity (delta x 100 x S x contracts). Buy expiry closest to 12 months (allowed range 9-18), strike rounded to the strike closest to 0.78 x S. Roll (sell to close, buy a new one) when: time to expiry < 120 days; delta > 0.95 (re-strike up, which locks in gains); delta < 0.70; or |delta-notional/Equity - L_t| > 0.5. When T = 0: sell everything and hold SGOV. Only trade if bid-ask/mid < 2%.
ideas.data: No free historical option quotes. The pre-2014 test must model prices with Black-Scholes, using VIX (free from CBOE/FRED, 1990-) plus a skew adjustment from the CBOE SKEW index (free, 1990-) for the 0.78-moneyness implied volatility, plus an assumed spread of 1% of premium. That is a model of the instrument, not real fills. Underlying: ^GSPC or SPY from Yahoo, with no survivorship issue.
ideas.testable_to_2014: Only partly. The signal can be tested to 2014; the option pricing is synthetic before and after 2014, because there is no free history at all. Real fills can only be checked forward, in paper trading.
ideas.expected_net: Compared with the baseline 3x ETF: + about 0.5-1.5%/yr from tax (11% vs 22%, with a separate deduction); - about 0.5-1.5%/yr from the embedded put premium and its skew on L x notional; - spread and roll costs (about 2-3 rolls a year x about 1% of premium, where premium is about 25-30% of notional, so about 0.3% of notional per roll); + something from avoiding daily-reset decay in choppy markets. Net expected difference about -1% to +1.5%/yr, Sharpe similar (about 0.4-0.5). Main benefit: no margin-call path, and the loss on a gap is capped at the premium.
ideas.capital_fit: Poor below 100M KRW. One SPY or QQQ call at delta 0.87 carries about USD 55-60k of delta-notional (about 80M KRW), so at 50M KRW a single contract is about 1.6x leverage and one step changes it by 1.6x. It only works at 100M+ or with lower-priced underlyings whose options are thin.
ideas.fake_risks: 1) Results depend on the assumed implied-volatility surface and spreads, which are not observed. 2) Treating US ETF options as overseas derivatives for tax is plausible but not confirmed. If they are taxed as overseas stocks at 22%, the main advantage disappears. 3) Contract lumpiness dominates at this capital size. 4) An apparent benefit could come from modelled skew that is cheaper than real quotes.

top_pick: Method 1, the tax-bucket and vehicle-routed Kelly-sized trend exposure. It takes the signal everyone has already tested and removes the drags the baseline pays for no reason: 22% tax with no loss carry-forward, unused second 2.5M KRW deduction, no ISA deferral, about 0.5% round-trip commission plus FX on every switch, and leverage stuck at 3x regardless of volatility. Most of the gain comes from statute and cost structure, not forecasting, so it is the most likely to survive the blind holdout. That is about +1.5 to +3.5%/yr of growth at 50-100M KRW and about +0.5 to +1.5% at 10M. Pre-register it as two arms on identical index paths: (A) baseline 3x ETF and 200-day trend filter, run through the full KRW tax engine; (B) Method 1. Testing on identical paths keeps the routing gain apart from any signal change. Add Method 2's sleeve only if capital reaches about 100M KRW and the 1981-2014 proxy test shows the combined Sharpe beating the core alone by more than 0.05.
honest_ceiling: Growth arithmetic: for a strategy with excess Sharpe S, the best long-run log growth comes at Kelly leverage, g* = r + S^2/2. At half Kelly, which is prudent because S is estimated with large error, g = r + 0.375*S^2. Plausible OUT-OF-SAMPLE Sharpe for what this investor can execute: an equity trend core at about 0.40-0.50, a diversified core plus trend sleeve at about 0.50-0.60. With r of about 3%: S=0.45 gives g* = 3 + 10.1 = 13.1% gross at full Kelly and 10.6% at half Kelly. S=0.60 gives 21% at full Kelly and 16.5% at half Kelly. Then subtract costs (about 0.5-1% routed, 2-4% for the baseline) and tax. Tax is 11-22% of positive years with no loss carry-forward, so the effective rate is about 15-25% of mean gains for a high-volatility strategy. That gives realistic expected NET growth of about 8-12%/yr in the central case and about 14-16%/yr if everything goes right (S=0.6, near Kelly, routed tax). Maximum drawdowns of -60% to -80% come with it. What 30% and 60% would require: net g = 30% means gross of about 30/0.85 + 1 = 36%, so S^2/2 = 0.33 and S = 0.81, sustained for decades after costs. 60% needs S = 1.2. No public, daily-frequency method on liquid indices that a retail account can run has a credible out-of-sample Sharpe near 0.8. Strategies that have one (market making, HFT, capacity-limited arbitrage) need infrastructure, data or counterparties this investor lacks. Luck is the only route: at Kelly with S=0.5, portfolio volatility is about 50%, so the standard deviation of realised annualised growth over 20 years is about 0.5/sqrt(20) = 11 points. A 30% outcome is then about 1.5-1.6 standard deviations above a central 12-13%, roughly a 5-7% chance, and it carries a matching chance of ending near zero. Small-capital note: at 10M KRW the two separate 2.5M KRW deductions plus the ISA's 2M KRW cover the first roughly 50-70% of yearly gains, so tax is almost irrelevant. There, the main levers are commission (get 0.07%), fewer switches, and continuous rather than 3x-fixed sizing.
assumptions_challenged: 1) Results judged pre-tax or with a flat tax. Korean tax is set per basket, per year, on realised gains, with no loss carry-forward. That penalises exactly the high-volatility, frequently switched 3x strategy. It also leaves two separate 2.5M KRW deductions (overseas stocks vs derivatives; confirmed by Income Tax Act art. 103 commentary), ISA deferral and the 11% derivatives rate unused. The vehicle is part of the strategy. 2) Leverage taken as a product (1x/2x/3x daily-reset ETF) rather than a continuous decision variable. Kelly says leverage should scale with expected excess return over variance, so it should fall when volatility is high and rise when it is low. 3) Each candidate judged standalone against the benchmark's CAGR. Under log growth, what matters is the gain in the PORTFOLIO's Sharpe, so a modest uncorrelated stream can be worth more than a higher-return correlated one. 4) A single historical CAGR used as the score. With -90% drawdowns acceptable and Kelly-like sizing, the right score is median and 10th-percentile terminal log wealth under block-bootstrapped paths and parameter uncertainty. A single path at 3x mostly measures luck. 5) Returns measured in USD. For a KRW investor, unhedged USD tends to rise in equity crises, lowering KRW volatility and raising the Kelly leverage, so the hedged and unhedged choice should be tested rather than assumed. 6) The 0.25% commission taken as fixed. With about 6 switches a year it costs about 3%/yr. Futures at about 0.01%, or a negotiated 0.07%, change the ranking of every high-turnover idea. 7) Wanting more alpha. With free data and daily execution, the remaining edge is mostly in removing frictions, not in finding signals. 8) A caution in the other direction: two tax facts need checking before relying on them. One web guide says Korea-listed DOMESTIC-index leveraged ETFs are taxed at 15.4% on the increase in their tax-base price, not exempt, though the actual tax is often small. Whether US-listed ETF options count as overseas exchange derivatives at 11% is plausible but not explicitly confirmed. Sources checked: https://glasswallet.com/blog/overseas-futures-tax-guide and https://etfshopping.com/guide/etf-tax
